title: Garbage sorting & neighbors
intro:
Garbage rules in Japan are strict and set by each municipality, so the rules in your new town may differ from what a friend in another city told you. When you register at the city office or move into your building, ask for the sorting guide and collection calendar. Many cities publish them in English and other languages, and some have apps that remind you what goes out each day.

Common categories include:

- {燃[も]えるゴミ} (burnable): food waste, paper scraps, many everyday items.
- {燃[も]えないゴミ} (non-burnable): things like ceramics, small metal items, broken glass.
- {資源[しげん]ゴミ} (recyclables): cans, glass bottles, PET bottles, paper and cardboard. Usually rinsed, with caps and labels removed.
- {粗大[そだい]ゴミ} (oversized items): furniture, bicycles and so on. You normally book a collection and pay by buying a sticker or ticket.

Some cities require designated bags ({指定袋[していぶくろ]}) sold at supermarkets and convenience stores. Put garbage out on the morning of collection day, at your building's designated spot, by the time on the calendar. Wrongly sorted bags may be left behind with a warning sticker. Large appliances such as TVs, refrigerators, washing machines and air conditioners are handled under a separate recycling system and cannot go out as ordinary garbage.

Good relations with neighbors matter. Greet people you meet, keep noise down at night (walls can be thin), and follow the garbage rules; these three things prevent most problems.

tips: Search for your city name plus {ゴミ} or the word garbage to find the official sorting guide; it is the only source that really counts.
When moving out, book oversized garbage collection early; around March and April slots fill up fast.
In apartment buildings, giving a small gift (such as a box of sweets or a hand towel) to the neighbors on each side when you move in is a nice gesture, though not everyone does it in big cities.
If you have a noise problem with a neighbor, it is usually better to contact the management company than to confront them directly.
Ask before putting out items you are unsure about. Neighbors and building managers would much rather you ask than guess.
